sections.title: Employment Contract
sections.text:
Nacho, an islander, here to help.

He couldn't think of a nicer way to put it, but he sincerely wants to help you.

sections.title: Token
sections.text: A small pouch made from a glove. He said he can only use one, so the other one...... Quick, say thank you to him, or he'll start wondering again whether it was rude to give you something he couldn't use.

sections.title: Profile
sections.text: Nacho, an Aegirian islander, proficient in hydrographic surveying and geographic modeling. After the Port City salvage project ended, he joined Rhodes Island on Clementia's recommendation, and is stationed in Iberia as a partner Operator, assisting Rhodes Island with hydrological observation and climate monitoring along the Iberian coast.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests reveal clear, normal outlines of internal organs, and no abnormal shadows have been detected. Originium granules have not been detected in the circulatory system and there is no sign of infection. At this time, this operator is believed to be uninfected.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 0%
Operator Homebound shows no signs of Originium infection.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.12u/L
Operator Homebound cooperated with us in completing the basic physical examination items, but for the items related to his special conditions (burns, amputated limb), he asked the Doctor to perform the examinations.
Along with those test results, the Doctor also brought a letter from Homebound. In the letter, he apologized over and over, trying to explain that asking the Doctor to perform those examinations wasn't aimed at the Medical Department; it was only because the Doctor could put him a little more at ease, but that wasn't our fault either, it was his own problem...
How should we tell him that always thinking so much isn't good for his health either?

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
"So, this is what you call practice makes perfect?"
When the curious HR Operator asked, Nacho's spherical probe was scanning a passage on Rhodes Island, near where a young patient's flying toy had gone missing. The device was originally used in Iberia to sense maritime weather and probe the structure of the seabed. On Nacho's fifth day at Rhodes Island, he stood outside the Engineering Department and made a modification request to the first Engineering Operator who greeted him. When the Engineering Operator asked why, he sheepishly pulled out three "Lost Item Retrieval Notices"—now the device can scan the basic spatial layout of any building or environment, and Nacho naturally became a volunteer at Lost and Found.
"I don't know why I lose so many things in a day either. It's not good to trouble the Operators at Lost and Found..." Nacho crouched down and held the scanning panel in front of the young patient. The child poked at the glowing spot: her toy was stuck in the ventilation duct. Nacho lay down on the floor by the wall and reached for it.
Nacho is undoubtedly a likable person. Though he looks like the cold air hovering over the Iberian sea and is missing an arm, he's very happy to help. However, whenever he runs into trouble of his own that he needs to deal with, he's not very good at asking others for help. Some of the older Operators who have gone on missions with him end up becoming his "guardians," in a sense.
"Oh!"
"Oh! You got little Lena's toy?"
"I think I might know why I lose so many things."
'Why?'
"When I worked at the Rea-Iberia salvage center, the technicians all wore diving suits when they went into the water. Even if they lost something, it'd just be lost inside the diving suit, and they could shake it out. That way, most personal belongings never got lost. But I always felt working like that was too inefficient, so I stuck my prosthetic out of the diving suit and worked directly in the seawater, and ended up losing a bolt, haha..."
"Haha?"
"And speaking of the prosthetic, I've figured out how to get the toy back. Could you use the weather sphere to distract little Lena?"
Nacho undid the clasp of his prosthetic. Detached from its owner's arm, the limb moved a few times under Nacho's remote control, then, like some Starpod creature, scrambled "every which way" into the duct and retrieved the toy. Even after it was reattached to Nacho, the HR Operator's terrified expression had yet to fade.
"Sorry, I didn't think I'd scare you too?"
"...Now I see why you have so many 'guardians.' I'd like to join them myself now. Even though it's only a prosthetic, attaching and detaching it still puts a strain on your body, so please don't do that so casually again."
"A part from this prosthetic once helped Supervisor Clementia recover Rea-Iberia, and made me a 'hero' in the eyes of some Iberians. That title makes me very, very uneasy. I'd much rather use it to recover a flying toy and be little Lena's 'hero.'"
“……”
"Hm? Why'd you go quiet?"
“……”
"I shouldn't talk either? Just accept your hug? O-okay..."

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
[Rhodes Island Internal Forum, Public Board: A Belated Apology]
I sincerely repent.
Last month, when I went to the Engineering Department for a meeting, I saw a young man planting sugarcane cuttings in a flowerpot. Thinking Rhodes Island's office environment improvement team was trying out some new enhancement again, I casually chatted with this sugarcane farmer for a bit. He was a little introverted, quite cute, and told me a lot of trivia about sugarcane seedlings and Iberian sandy loam and the like. Good thing he kept me company, or I'd have had no idea what to say when I first met Mr. Nacho, the Port City's lead hydrographic surveying technician. Sugarcane might make a good topic, I thought. Well, I suppose some of you reading this have already figured out the mistake I made. But last month, foolish me only realized he was Mr. Nacho when the "sugarcane farmer" finished hauling five bags of sandy loam himself, sat down in front of me catching his breath, and pulled out the engineering plan...

Reply: Hahaha, are all engineering people that multi-talented?
Reply: Stop laughing. I already feel guilty enough.
Reply: Don't worry too much about it. People from every department love hanging around Engineering, so mistaking someone is normal. Yesterday I went to Engineering to wait for the engineer I was liaising with, and after ages all I saw was the curly-haired guy who serves food in the cafeteria going into the office. Maybe he was there to collect sugarcane, haha.
Reply: Curly-haired guy... is he Aegirian, with a prosthetic right arm?
Reply: Yeah. Huh, how did you know?
Reply: ...

In just one week, the replies under the apology post about mistaking Nacho kept piling up. People speculated about this Operator's identity, the discussion strayed completely from the original poster's intent, and the final conclusion was that Nacho is a humanoid weapon secretly developed by Columbia: the One-Armed Iron Man. The matter only came to an end after Nacho himself saw the post, apologized to the original poster, and nearly made his own résumé public.
Before joining Rhodes Island, Nacho had worked no fewer than twenty different jobs: sugarcane farmer, sugar distributor, net weaver, locksmith, acolyte... Between each job there was a gap, long or short. When we asked Nacho, we learned that most of those "gaps" were because he was cooperating with Inquisition summonses over matters concerning his fellow islanders, or because the phantom pain of his severed limb grew worse and he had to seek further treatment. Although Iberia has set out on the road to reform, it can be surmised that before this, many of Nacho's career changes may have been related to ostracism by Iberian commoners. Nacho's response to this was simple: apart from force majeure, the most important reason he changed jobs so often was to let Iberians see that he, too, was an ordinary Iberian, that he, too, was working for Iberia. Some of his fellow islanders—even the person who was once his best friend—believe this craving for acceptance is just currying favor with Iberians and will not bring true equality to the islanders. But as Nacho sees it, setting aside all the complicated calculations and incitements of old grudges, his varied work experience taught him how to live well in Iberia, especially after his grandmother Rufina passed away.

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
We nearly came to blows.
When we learned that Rufina's grandson was safe and that she was willing to raise him, we were all actually very happy. During the three months she agonized over what to name him, we all helped think of names too. But no one expected that in the end, what she decided on would be an Iberian name.
It's not that islanders can't take Iberian names. Too many of our people have forgotten our ancestors' naming customs and had no choice but to use Iberian names; that's nothing unusual. But Rufina? She, of all people, would never do that.
In the end, the reason we gather here to discuss how to resist and how to struggle is all because of Rufina. If not for her, we'd probably have just stood by and watched as one fellow islander after another was stabbed to death, burned to death, nailed to lampposts.
Rufina never accepted this reality. Islanders contributed to Iberia; islanders did not bring disaster upon Iberia—she spent the latter half of her life trying to prove this. She told each of us to remember everything about Aegir, because if we didn't remember, no one ever would again.
And then she gave her own grandson a thoroughly Iberian name?
The most radical young people among us even suspected she had betrayed us. That night, no matter how people accused her, Rufina said nothing. Only at the end, when everyone had argued themselves hoarse, did she toss out a single remark:
"Whatever I want to prove, it has nothing to do with that child."
After that, she never acted together with us again.
—An islander who once took part in acts of sabotage

"Name?"
"Nacho."
"Surname?"
"Uh... García López."
"Paternal surname first, or maternal surname first?"
"Uh, no. My parents both had Aegirian names. My given name and surname were both made up by Grandma out of thin air, the most ordinary, most common ones, so I'd seem more like an Iberian..."
"Understood. Then would you like to change your registered name? We can take care of it."
"N-no, it's fine. The current name is good. I really like it. Even though it doesn't actually change how anyone sees me... the name itself is nice."
"Okay."
"But if possible... I'd still like the record to leave out the surname and just say 'Nacho.' That way it'd be better for everyone..."
"Better for everyone? Why?"
—HR Department Registration Office, a conversation

What Nacho borrows most here is always technical manuals, and sometimes novels too. But lately, he's been borrowing fewer and fewer novels, and more and more scripts.
Looking at the books he returns, it's not hard to see why. All the novels he's read, though he clearly tried hard to smooth the pages flat, show the first few dozen pages much more puffed up than the rest; he probably flipped back through the opening section again and again. But with a script, the traces of repeated flipping are confined to the cast list at the very front.
My guess is that Nacho must be very bad at remembering names. With a novel, after reading just two pages he'd have to flip back to figure out who's who; by comparison, the nice thing about a script is that all the characters' names are neatly listed right at the front.
Ha, if everyone's name in the book were as short and easy to remember as "Nacho," he'd surely have an easier time reading.
—The Rhodes Island library administrator

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
[Unofficial record of the Rhodes Island Rea-Iberia Office]
Three days ago at dawn, when I saw the leader of a radical islander movement wanted by the Inquisition walk out of Nacho's room, I should have worried first about Nacho García López's personal safety. But to be honest, the first thought that came into my head was how the cooperation between Rhodes Island and the Inquisition would end up.
I read the report Operator Clementia submitted to Rhodes Island. It recorded in detail a series of incidents during the salvage of the Port City, and also mentioned Nacho's contributions to the salvage and to the recovery of Rea-Iberia's central district. I saw that this city, which Nacho named "Our Iberia" on the nautical chart, is being rebuilt, and I saw that shops along the streets no longer treat islanders and Iberians differently. But that doesn't mean the islander question has been fully resolved in Iberia. Even in the Port City, even after witnessing with their own eyes islanders and Iberians salvaging together, some still choose to fight, and that unsettles me.
So I lost my composure. I angrily demanded whether Nacho had violated Rhodes Island's code of conduct, suspecting he was colluding with radicals. But he just waited for me to finish venting, then told me everything they had talked about that night, in full detail.
All night, they didn't say a single word about the Port City or the situation in Iberia. They only shared memories. Each of them had lost several family members and friends, had lost several jobs that might have let them live a steady life, had learned to sail and then been forbidden from sailing. They talked about whose relatives among their fellow islanders might have made the glowing objects atop the semaphore tower in the Port City's central district, and how the seaweed wine here differs from that elsewhere in Iberia.
I didn't understand how these topics could keep them talking all night. No, actually, I do understand. As an Aegirian also born in Iberia, I know well that chances to talk with others as equals are few, which is also why I left my hometown early and came to Rhodes Island. When I learned that an islander had found what was once Iberia's most prosperous capital using a single bolt left behind by a family member, I was astonished. What astonished me wasn't how much luck and effort it took to achieve that, but that Nacho, as one of those who had been ostracized, was actually willing to do it.
Nacho told me that the radical who came looking for him did want his help, but he had only promised not to tell the Inquisition about them, and had agreed to nothing else. Without disgust, without fear, without worry, without any of the emotions I felt when I left Iberia or when I heard radicals had come to the office, Nacho calmly told me he would never bring the islanders' problems to Rhodes Island, because protecting the islanders was his choice, and joining Rhodes Island was another, unrelated choice.
He noticed my dejection and guilt and sat with me by the sea for a long time. Before leaving, he patted my hand with his prosthetic, still a little unaccustomed to it, and told me I'd done well.

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
The condition of Nacho's arm is worrying.
Since his promotion, his sense of responsibility seems to have grown even stronger. Nacho actively takes part in all kinds of affairs between Rhodes Island and Iberia. Hydrographic surveying already puts a strain on his prosthetic, and these days he comes to you for prosthetic maintenance more and more often...
"It's fine to take on the responsibilities of my new work slowly, at my own pace? But—"
"No, no, no, I'm not worried Rhodes Island won't pay extra, and I'm not worried the quality of the lubricant will drop. I'm only working overtime to—uh, I'm only working overtime because..."
"Even if my pay has gone up, and there's more I can do and more I have to do, the time we spend together is still just this one hour each month for maintaining my prosthetic, isn't it?"
"If working overtime could increase the maintenance time... ow, please don't knock me on the head..."
"What else do I want to do besides maintenance? Together with you?!"
"I-I haven't thought about it yet... I'll come up with something soon."
